QF.id: SIA Case Studies on SAS Standards_14

question.text: Under SAS-200 a rural maternal-health programme reports 60% reduction in maternal mortality in beneficiary villages (NGO Sakhi case in Chapter 8). Before accepting this, the SIA should FIRST:

answer.text: Accept the figure if signed off by the CFO of the SE

Check whether baseline maternal-mortality was statistically measurable in the small village sample — for low-frequency events small-sample volatility can produce a 60% swing without real programme effect
Convert the 60% into a monetised DALY figure and include in SROI
Benchmark against the national SRS average and adopt whichever is higher

explanation.text: **The Logic:** Maternal mortality is a low-frequency event; in a small beneficiary pool (say 120 villages, few hundred pregnancies each) a one or two-death swing can show as a 60% fall with no real causation. Under SAS-200 the SIA must test statistical significance and confidence interval before accepting. **The Trap:** Option A abandons professional scepticism. Option C jumps to valuation without first validating the input. Option D is indicator-shopping. **Cross-Exam Context:** Similar small-sample volatility appears in XV (Research Analyst — survey sample sizing) and III-C (Compliance — statistical testing). **Assessor's Pro-Tip:** For any mortality / low-prevalence indicator, reject percentage-point claims unless confidence intervals are reported. Push the SE to give you absolute numbers plus the 95% CI.
